subtype: Restless at work and searching for stimulation [Actor]
passage: You want to know the real reason I asked for that new project, Nitin? Last year at the bank I had the same five reconciliations every morning. Done by eleven. After that I'd refresh the news, rearrange my desktop icons, make tea I didn't want, walk to the printer for nothing. By evening I'd feel this low, sticky guilt, like I'd stolen a salary. I thought I was just lazy. Then one day my manager handed me a messy data problem nobody else wanted, and I didn't look at my phone for three hours. I wasn't lazy. I was starving for something hard. So I asked for more of that. On weeks when I'm properly tired, though, I take the afternoon slow. Different hunger. Anyway, that's Varun's big secret.

qa.q: By what time did Varun finish the five reconciliations?
qa.a: By eleven.

qa.q: Why did Varun feel a low, sticky guilt by evening?
qa.a: Filling the hours with small distractions felt like not earning the salary, and Varun blamed laziness, not yet seeing that the work was simply too easy.

qa.q: What choice turned Varun's boredom into energy?
qa.a: Asking for more hard problems after noticing three focused hours on the messy data, while resting instead on weeks of real tiredness.

qa.q: How might Varun's manager see the change after the messy data problem?
qa.a: The manager probably sees an employee who was coasting become eager and focused, and may be glad to have someone who wants the tough work.

grounding: An under-challenged adult fills workdays with small distractions and guilt, then finds the boredom was asking for difficulty.

subtype: Restless at work and searching for stimulation [Actor]
passage: I'm Pankaj, and Hrithik sits two desks from me at the logistics office. For the last month I've watched him do something odd. He finishes his tracking sheet by noon, then spends the afternoon on small things: lining up every pen, checking cricket scores, walking to the pantry four times, rereading old emails. He jokes loudly, but when the boss walks past he quickly opens a spreadsheet and looks guilty. I'm not sure what's going on with him. Maybe he's tired, maybe he's bored out of his mind. Last Friday I asked him, lightly, "Too little work, or too little sleep?" He thought for a while. "Too little that matters," he said. On Monday he asked the boss if he could take on planning the new warehouse routes.

qa.q: What does Hrithik finish by noon?
qa.a: His tracking sheet.

qa.q: What does Hrithik's guilty look when the boss passes suggest?
qa.a: He seems to feel he is wasting paid time; the distractions don't satisfy him, and he is uneasy about being seen filling the day with nothing.

qa.q: Which question helped Hrithik work out what his boredom needed?
qa.a: Pankaj's light "too little work, or too little sleep?", which let Hrithik name the real gap, work that matters, and then ask for the route planning.

qa.q: How does Pankaj see Hrithik's afternoons, and what can't Pankaj be sure of?
qa.a: Pankaj sees the pens, pantry trips and loud jokes, but can't tell from outside whether Hrithik is tired or bored until he answers the question.

grounding: A colleague observes an unchallenged worker filling afternoons with small distractions and guilt until he asks for meaningful work.

subtype: Restless at work and searching for stimulation [Actor]

Wednesday: "When did you last sleep properly?" Hafsa asked. Nitin counted back. His cousin's wedding, two late nights, a long Sunday drive. "Maybe the poster isn't boring," she said. "Maybe you're just empty."
Saturday: Nitin slept till nine, went for a slow walk and didn't open his laptop.
The next Monday he opened the poster brief first thing. It was the same brief. But it held him for two hours, and he didn't open a single other tab.

qa.a: Hafsa's question about sleep; Nitin chose a restful Saturday instead of forcing himself, and on Monday the same brief held his attention.

qa.a: Where Nitin sees a dull project, Hafsa sees an exhausted colleague, noticing the yawns and guessing he needs rest rather than excitement.

passage: After the temple fair in Hatta, Payal came home with a wooden puzzle from the toy stall: fifteen pieces that had to make a bullock cart. She sat on the verandah floor with it while her mother, Vandana, went to milk the buffalo. The wheels were easy. The cart body was not. Payal turned one piece every way, frowned, tried another. The shadows moved across the steps. Vandana called twice that the rotis were ready; Payal didn't hear either time. When the last piece slid in, she clapped once, loudly, and only then noticed her stomach growling and the lamp already lit. "I thought it was still afternoon," she told Vandana, grinning so wide her cheeks hurt.

qa.q: How many pieces did the wooden puzzle have?
qa.a: Fifteen pieces, making a bullock cart.

qa.a: It had easy parts and a harder part she could just manage with patience, so it kept her working without making her give up.

qa.a: Vandana may have been puzzled or a little annoyed at first, then amused to see her daughter so lost in the puzzle she thought it was still afternoon.

His grandmother set a bowl of noodles beside him; they went cold. At half past two a marble rolled all the way down, clicked through both spirals and dropped into the cup. Tuan looked at the clock and his mouth fell open. "Where did the day go?"

qa.a: The big design with the double spiral.

passage:
Thursday night
Weirdest thing. I came home furious after the maths test, slammed my door, and picked up the guitar just to make noise. Farida ma'am gave us that new fingerpicking pattern last week, the one that's a bit too fast for me. I started slow. Then a little faster. Then I missed, went back, got it. I don't know how long I played. When I looked up, the room was dark and my phone had eleven messages I never heard. And the anger was just gone. Not pushed down, gone. My head felt clear, like after rain. I think the pattern needed every bit of me, but I could still just about get it, so there was no room left for the maths test.
Deepika

passage: In Saurabh's village near Wardha, the Ganesh festival was two weeks away, and his uncle had given him a new tabla rhythm for the procession, one step harder than anything he'd played. After school he sat on the cot under the neem tree and began. Wrong. Again. Slower. The goats wandered past, the school bus honked on the road, the neighbour's radio played. Saurabh didn't notice any of it. His phone, left on the windowsill, buzzed with the class group; he never looked. Chetan came over to call him for cricket, stood watching for a while, then just sat down. When Saurabh finally stopped, the sun was low and his palms tingled. "You played for two hours," Chetan said. Saurabh blinked. He felt light, and oddly peaceful.

qa.q: Where did Saurabh sit to practise?

passage: People ask how I got so much done this quarter. Honestly, I stopped waiting for good days and started building them. I'm Deepika, I write code for a logistics firm, and until March my mornings were chaos: chat pings, email, "quick calls". Then my lead, Farida, sat with me and we made three rules. One: each morning I write a single clear goal on a sticky note, like "finish the route-sorting function", not "work on project". Two: from nine to eleven, notifications off and a sign on my chair. Three: I pick a task that stretches me a little, not the easy tickets I used to hide in. The first week felt awkward. By the third, those two hours were the best part of my day. I'd look up and it'd be eleven already.

qa.q: What are Deepika's protected hours each morning?
qa.a: From nine to eleven, with notifications off and a sign on the chair.

qa.q: Why did Deepika use to hide in the easy tickets?
qa.a: Easy tickets felt safe and quick, but they gave nothing to sink into, so the mornings stayed scattered and unsatisfying.

qa.q: Which of the three rules might matter most, and why?
qa.a: Picking a task that stretches a little, because without challenge the quiet hours would still feel dull; the clear goal and silence make that stretch workable.

qa.q: How might Farida see the change in Deepika's work?
qa.a: Farida likely sees more finished work and a more engaged coder, and is pleased that the rules they built together are paying off.

grounding: An adult builds conditions for deep focus with clear goals, fewer interruptions and slightly harder tasks.

passage: I'm Divyansh, and I share an office with Binita at the translation agency. Last year she was always frazzled, answering calls while translating, jumping between five documents. This year something changed, and I've been paying attention. Every morning she writes one line on a card, something like "finish chapter 4 of the Marathi manual". Then she puts her phone in a drawer and hangs a small "deep work till 12" sign on her chair. She's also started taking the harder literary jobs she used to pass to seniors. I can't tell exactly what she's feeling, but around eleven she goes very still, lips moving slightly, and doesn't notice me walking past. At lunch she seems lighter. When I asked, she said, "I stopped hoping for focus and started setting it up."

qa.a: A small "deep work till 12" sign.

qa.q: What does Binita's stillness around eleven suggest about her state?
qa.a: She seems fully absorbed in the work, so focused she doesn't notice Divyansh; seeming lighter at lunch suggests it feels good.

qa.q: Which of Binita's choices would you advise a frazzled colleague to copy first?
qa.a: Writing one clear goal on a card and putting the phone away, since those make the harder jobs possible without constant interruption.

qa.q: How does Divyansh's view of Binita change from last year to this year?
qa.a: Divyansh once saw a frazzled colleague juggling calls and files, and now sees someone calm and absorbed, though only able to guess at her inner state.

passage: Zubin, you said "whatever" about your spelling test. I know that word. When I was nine, in Jabalpur, I had a teacher who shouted at every wrong sum. "Ritu, wrong again!" I'd try, get it wrong, get shouted at. Try harder, still wrong, still shouted at. One day I simply stopped. When she asked for my answer I said "I don't know" before even reading the question. Why try, if trying and not trying ended the same way? It felt almost clever, like I'd found a way to hurt less. It took a different teacher, two years later, praising one right step at a time, before I believed my effort could change anything. So when you say whatever, beta, I don't hear lazy. I hear tired of losing.

qa.q: What would the teacher shout when young Ritu got a sum wrong?
qa.a: "Ritu, wrong again!"

qa.q: Why did not trying feel almost clever to young Ritu?
qa.a: Trying and not trying ended the same way, with shouting, so giving up seemed a sensible way to hurt less.

qa.q: What turning point helped Ritu start trying again?
qa.a: A new teacher two years later who praised one right step at a time, which showed that effort could make a difference.

qa.q: How might Zubin feel hearing "I don't hear lazy"?
qa.a: Zubin may feel understood rather than scolded, and more willing to talk about why the spelling test feels pointless.

grounding: An elder recalls giving up on maths at nine when effort never changed the outcome, making passivity feel sensible.

passage: Dilnaz had one old bicycle, her brother's, too tall for her, and only the narrow lane behind the flats to practise in, between parked scooters. Every evening for two weeks she tried. Every evening she wobbled, scraped a knee or bumped a scooter, and the watchman shouted. Her cousins laughed from the balcony. On Saturday Maria from the next building came down with her own small bike. "Want to try mine? It's lower." Dilnaz didn't even look up from the step. "Whatever. I can't ride. I'll never ride." "You haven't tried this one." "Doesn't matter. I always fall." Maria sat beside her, turning a pedal with her hand. Dilnaz picked at the scab on her knee and stared at the gutter.

qa.q: Where did Dilnaz practise riding?
qa.a: In the narrow lane behind the flats, between parked scooters.

qa.q: Why did Dilnaz refuse Maria's lower bike without even looking up?

qa.q: How might Maria feel sitting beside Dilnaz?
qa.a: Maria probably wants to help and may feel a little hurt by the "whatever", but sitting close shows she hasn't given up on Dilnaz.

grounding: A child who kept failing on a too-tall bike in a cramped lane stops trying and says 'whatever'.

passage: In the Lajpat Nagar flat, Simran's English notebook was mostly red. Every essay came back with "careless!" across the top, however long she spent on it. In August she rewrote one three times; it still came back red. So in September she stopped. When her Rekha masi, visiting from Jaipur, asked about the new essay, Simran shrugged. "Whatever. It'll be wrong anyway." She had written two lines and drawn a cat. "Did you even try?" Rekha asked. "Why would I? Trying and not trying get the same marks." Simran said it calmly, as if explaining the weather. Rekha looked through the old essays, saw how neat the rewritten one was, and felt her throat tighten.

qa.q: How many times did Simran rewrite the August essay?
qa.a: Three times; it still came back red.

qa.q: Why does Simran say it so calmly, as if explaining the weather?
qa.a: To her it is a plain fact that effort changes nothing, so giving up feels sensible rather than upsetting.

qa.q: What could Rekha masi do next to help Simran?
qa.a: Point to one specific thing that improved in the neat rewrite, and help her talk to the teacher about what "careless" means, so effort can be linked to results.

qa.q: What does Rekha feel when she sees the rewritten essay?
qa.a: Her throat tightens as she realises Simran worked hard and was still marked down, so the "whatever" hides disappointment, not laziness.

grounding: A child whose repeated effort keeps getting the same red marks stops trying and says it won't matter.

subtype: Not asking for help at home [Actor]
passage: For years, whenever I asked for something at home, a cycle, a phone of my own, a place on the school trip, the answer was "not now" or nothing at all, because my grandmother was ill and everyone was stretched thin. So I stopped asking. Last month my parents actually asked me what I wanted for my seventeenth birthday, and my mouth just opened and closed. I said, "Nothing, anything's fine." My friend Rehana couldn't believe it. "Jyoti, they're asking! Things are okay at your place now." I know that. My head knows that. But part of me still waits quietly, as if asking is a door that doesn't open. I'm trying to say one small want out loud each week. This week it was "Can we have dosa on Sunday?" We did.

qa.q: What did Jyoti ask for this week?
qa.a: "Can we have dosa on Sunday?"

qa.q: Why did Jyoti's mouth just open and close when asked about the birthday?
qa.a: After years of "not now", Jyoti had stopped expecting wishes to matter, so even a genuine offer found nothing ready to say.

qa.q: What choice is Jyoti making to change the old belief?
qa.a: Saying one small want out loud each week, so each yes, like the Sunday dosa, becomes proof that asking can work now.

qa.q: How might Jyoti's parents feel hearing "Nothing, anything's fine"?
qa.a: They may feel puzzled or sad, having finally been able to ask, and not realise their child learned to stop asking during the hard years.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Maria, Class 10 check-ins, 3 October
Dilnaz came in about her falling science marks. When I asked if anyone at home could help, she said, "I don't ask them for things." She explained, flatly, that for years her requests went unanswered while her parents worked double shifts; now her mother has a daytime job and is home in the evenings, but Dilnaz still doesn't ask. She sat with her hands tucked under her legs and looked at the floor. She didn't seem upset, more resigned, as if asking had stopped being an option.
What I did: we practised one sentence she could say at home tonight: "Can you sit with me for my science for twenty minutes?" She agreed to try once and tell me on Friday. With her permission, I'll also phone her mother.

passage: In the statistics tutorial at her Toronto college, Soo-ah had noticed Leila right away: sharp questions in week one, then silence. Soo-ah gave her another, slightly harder. Right again. By the end of the hour Leila had done four and was frowning at the fifth by choice. Soo-ah said nothing about it, only ticked the page.

passage: At the polytechnic workshop, Preeti ma'am watched Vijay stand at his bench with his arms folded while the others started on the circuit board. "Why aren't you starting?" "No point, ma'am. Mine never works. Last three boards, all failed." Preeti knew his theory marks were among the best in the class. She also knew how the last three boards had gone: one bad solder each time, and laughter from the next bench when the last one smoked. So she took away the full board and handed him a small strip. "Just solder these four joints. Nothing else." He did it, grumbling. She tested them: perfect. "Now these four." Also perfect. By the end of the session he'd finished the whole power section, and he was the one asking for the next task.

qa.a: A small strip, with four joints to solder.

qa.q: Why did Vijay stand with his arms folded instead of starting?

qa.q: Which choice by Preeti ma'am changed the session?

passage:
Dear Ujjwal,
I noticed something in class on Monday and wanted to write rather than mention it in front of everyone. When I handed out the essay prompt, you wrote "I can't write essays" at the top of the page and put your pen down. You've said this before. But I've read your lab reports, and they are clear and well argued. So here's my suggestion for this week: don't write the essay. Write only the first paragraph, the one that says what you think and why, and bring it to my office on Thursday. That's all. One paragraph is something I know you can manage. If it goes the way I expect, we'll add the second next week.
Best,
Parveen Qureshi
Lecturer, English Communication

qa.q: What did Ujjwal write at the top of the essay prompt?
qa.a: "I can't write essays."

qa.q: What might Ujjwal be feeling when the pen goes down?
qa.a: Ujjwal likely feels defeated in advance, sure that effort on an essay will fail again, so stopping feels safer than trying.

qa.q: What choice does Parveen make, and why might it work?
qa.a: Asking for just one paragraph, a task Ujjwal can succeed at, so a real success can start to break the belief that effort is useless.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal feel reading that the lab reports are clear and well argued?
qa.a: Ujjwal may feel surprised and quietly encouraged that a lecturer noticed real skill, which makes the one-paragraph task feel possible.

grounding: A lecturer notices a capable student give up before starting and writes to set one small, achievable task.

subtype: Stuck in an unresponsive job or home [Actor]
passage: At the small branch office in Latur, Saurabh had asked for a working laptop four times since January. The first request got a "we'll see". The second, silence. By the fourth, he wrote it half-heartedly and never followed up. His salary went home to help with his sister's college fees, so leaving wasn't an option. By June he'd stopped asking for anything, not leave, not a fan for the stuffy back room. He came in, did what he could on the shared computer, went home and lay on the bed. Chetan, his old college friend, noticed on their weekly call that he said "doesn't matter" to everything, even cricket. "You sound flat, yaar. For months now." Saurabh didn't argue. Chetan sent him the number of a counsellor and stayed on the line while he saved it.

qa.q: How many times had Saurabh asked for a working laptop?
qa.a: Four times since January.

qa.q: Why did Saurabh stop asking for anything, even a fan?
qa.a: Every request met silence or a vague answer, so asking felt useless, and with leaving not possible, giving up seemed like the only sensible way to cope.

qa.q: What turning point could help Saurabh, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Chetan naming the months of flatness and staying on the line while Saurabh saved the counsellor's number; a trained person can help when a heavy mood lasts.

qa.q: How does Chetan experience the weekly calls?
qa.a: Chetan hears an old friend say "doesn't matter" to everything, even cricket, and is worried enough to act rather than just listen.

grounding: An adult whose repeated requests are ignored, and who cannot leave, stops asking and feels flat, and a friend points to a counsellor.

subtype: Stuck in an unresponsive job or home [Actor]
passage: Reena worked from home in the family's crowded flat in Bhopal, where her requests had a way of disappearing. A small desk in the corner: "later". Quiet between ten and one for client calls: nodded at, then forgotten, with the TV blaring. She had asked for a year. Lately she didn't. She took calls in the stairwell, ate standing up, and when her mother asked what she wanted for dinner, she said "anything" in the same flat tone she used for everything. Her brother Yusuf, home for Eid, noticed she didn't laugh at his jokes, didn't argue, didn't seem to want anything at all. That evening on the terrace he asked how long she'd felt like this. "Months," she said. "I just don't feel much." He said talking to a counsellor might help, and offered to sit with her while she called.

qa.q: Where did Reena take her client calls?
qa.a: In the stairwell.

qa.q: What does Reena's flat "anything" suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: After a year of ignored requests she has stopped expecting anything to change, and the feeling has spread into numbness about everything, even dinner.

qa.q: What choice by Yusuf is a wise next step?
qa.a: Asking how long she has felt this way and suggesting a counsellor, then offering to sit with her while she calls, since a heavy mood lasting months deserves trained help.

qa.q: How does Yusuf see his sister during the Eid visit?
qa.a: Yusuf notices she no longer laughs, argues or wants anything, and the change worries him enough to ask gently on the terrace.

grounding: An adult whose requests at home have been ignored for a year stops asking and feels numb, and her brother suggests a counsellor.

passage:
"Hemant, you didn't ask about the transfer?"
"No point, bhaiya."
Omkar put down the newspaper. "You were so sure in March."
"I asked in March. And May. And July. Each time: 'We'll look into it.' Nobody looked into anything." Hemant shrugged. "So I stopped."
"You could go above your manager."
"Why? Same answer."
"You've been saying 'why' to everything lately. Even the trek."
"I just don't feel like anything, bhaiya. Everything's grey."
Omkar was quiet. "How long has it been grey?"
"Since spring, maybe."
"That's a long time. Will you talk to someone about it? A counsellor, a doctor, someone trained. I'll come with you to book it."
Hemant looked at him for a long moment. "Tomorrow?"
"Tomorrow."

qa.q: In which months did Hemant ask about the transfer?
qa.a: In March, May and July.

qa.q: Why does Hemant say "No point" about asking again?
qa.a: Each request got "We'll look into it" and nothing happened, so he has come to believe asking changes nothing, and the greyness has spread to everything.

qa.q: What choice by Omkar helps, and why?
qa.a: Asking how long it has been grey, then suggesting a trained counsellor or doctor and offering to go along, because a low mood lasting months needs more than a pep talk.

qa.q: How might Omkar feel hearing that Hemant doesn't even want the trek?
qa.a: Omkar is likely worried, since losing interest in things Hemant used to enjoy shows the problem is bigger than one transfer.

grounding: An adult whose repeated requests at work are ignored stops asking and feels grey, and his brother offers to help him see a professional.

passage: I'm Manjula, and I live in the flat below Devika's. This summer she asked her mother for one pot on their balcony, all to herself. She chose the seeds, tomato, from a packet at the market, and decided where the pot would go: the sunny corner, not the shady one her mother suggested. Every morning I'd hear her little watering can, and sometimes her voice counting leaves. When the first flower came, she ran down the stairs to show me. When the first tomato turned red, she brought it to me on a steel plate, very serious. "I grew it. I picked the corner," she said. I don't know everything she was thinking, but she stood taller than I'd seen before.

qa.q: Where did Devika decide to put her pot?
qa.a: In the sunny corner, not the shady one her mother suggested.

qa.q: Why does Devika say "I picked the corner" so seriously?
qa.a: She is proud that her own choice worked; the red tomato shows her that what she decided made something happen.

qa.q: What choice by Devika's mother helped Devika learn that her actions matter?
qa.a: Letting Devika choose the seeds and the spot, even against her own suggestion, so the result clearly belonged to Devika.

qa.q: How does Manjula experience Devika's summer?
qa.a: Manjula hears the daily watering and gets shown every stage, and sees Devika standing taller, though only guessing at her thoughts.

grounding: A neighbour watches a child choose and tend a tomato plant and grow more confident when her choice works.

passage:

Monday: After school Zubin opened the car again, on his own this time. He found a wire loose from the battery box. He pushed it back and pressed it down with tape. The wheels twitched once, then stopped. He frowned, pressed harder, tried again. Whirr. The car shot across the floor.
Thursday: When his friend's torch stopped working, Zubin said, "Let me look," before anyone else could. He opened it, turned the batteries round, and it lit up. He grinned all the way home.

qa.q: What did Zubin find wrong with the car on Monday?
qa.a: A wire loose from the battery box.

qa.q: Why did Zubin say "Let me look" so quickly on Thursday?
qa.a: Fixing the car had shown him his efforts could work, so he felt confident and eager to try again.

qa.q: Which choice by Afreen didi helped Zubin most?
qa.a: Handing him the screwdriver instead of fixing it herself, so the success on Monday was his own.

qa.q: How might Afreen didi feel hearing about the torch on Thursday?

grounding: Over a week a child who fixes his own toy learns his actions matter and offers to fix a friend's torch.

passage: Mehak, come, look at this mango tree. When I was seven, I spat a mango seed into the corner of this yard and asked my father if I could keep it there. He said, "It's yours. You decide." So I decided everything. I put a ring of bricks round it so the goats wouldn't eat it. I carried water from the well in a small brass lota every evening, even when it rained, because I wasn't sure rain counted. When the first two leaves came up, I ran to tell everyone in the lane. Nobody else cared much, but I did. That's when I learned that if I did something, something happened. Disha's tree, they called it. Sixty years, and it still gives mangoes. Now, which pot do you want for your chilli seeds?

qa.q: What did young Disha put round the seed to protect it?
qa.a: A ring of bricks, so the goats wouldn't eat it.

qa.q: Why did young Disha keep watering even when it rained?
qa.a: Disha wasn't sure the rain counted and wanted to be certain the tree got its care; being in charge made every choice feel important.

qa.q: What choice by the father made the lesson possible?
qa.a: Saying "It's yours. You decide", which gave the child real decisions and a result to see.

qa.q: What might Mehak feel when asked to choose a pot for the chilli seeds?
qa.a: Mehak may feel trusted and excited, being handed the same kind of choice that made the mango tree so special.

grounding: An elder recalls how choosing and tending a mango seed as a child showed the child that actions could make things happen.

passage: The week his parents told him they were separating, Javier couldn't focus on anything. At night in his room in Madrid he lay listening to their low voices downstairs. On Thursday his friend Chen found him staring at a blank maths book in the library. "You can't fix their thing," Chen said. "But what can you fix?" They tore out a page and drew a line down the middle. On one side Javier wrote: "whether they split up; where Dad lives; what they argue about." On the other: "my homework hour; football on Saturdays; talking to the school counsellor; calling Abuela." He looked at the second list for a long time. That evening he did his homework hour and called his grandmother. It didn't fix anything big. But he slept.

qa.q: What did Javier write on the second side of the page?
qa.a: "My homework hour; football on Saturdays; talking to the school counsellor; calling Abuela."

qa.q: Why might Javier have looked at the second list for a long time?
qa.a: After a week of feeling powerless, seeing things he could actually do probably felt like relief, a small piece of control back.

qa.q: Which choice helped Javier that evening, and why?
qa.a: Acting on two items from the second list, the homework hour and calling his grandmother; doing something he could control eased the helpless feeling.

qa.q: How might Chen feel seeing the list filled in?
qa.a: Chen may feel glad to have found a practical way to help a friend through something neither of them can fix.

grounding: A teenager facing his parents' separation lists what he can and cannot control and acts on the first list.

passage: In the counsellor's room at St. Agnes High, Chinmay sat hunched in the plastic chair. His father had lost his job in March, and home had become quiet and tense. "I can't do anything," he said. "Everything's just happening to us." Mr Thomas, the counsellor, handed him a sheet with two boxes. "Let's sort it. What's outside your control? What's inside?" Chinmay filled the first box fast: Papa's job, money, Mummy's worry, the rent. The second took longer: his study timetable, cricket practice, helping his little sister with homework, talking to Mr Thomas on Fridays, telling his uncle how he felt. "Pick one from the second box for this week," Mr Thomas said. Chinmay picked the timetable. On Friday he came back with it filled in, and sat up straighter.

qa.q: What did Chinmay pick from the second box for the week?
qa.a: The study timetable.

qa.q: What was Chinmay feeling when he said "Everything's just happening to us"?
qa.a: He felt powerless; the job loss and tension at home seemed to leave him no part to play.

qa.q: Which choice by Mr Thomas helped Chinmay, and why?
qa.a: Asking him to sort worries into two boxes and pick just one controllable action, which turned a vague weight into one step he could take.

qa.q: How might Chinmay's little sister be affected by his second box?
qa.a: If he helps with her homework, she gets support from her brother during a tense time at home, and may feel steadier too.

grounding: A counsellor helps a teenager in a tense family situation sort what he can control and act on it.

passage:
Dear Sonali,
You asked why I've been so quiet on our calls. Nani moved in with us after her fall, and the house is different now. Mummy is tired all the time, and there are arguments about money that I'm not supposed to hear. For weeks I felt useless, like everything was happening around me and I was just a piece of furniture. Then our class teacher told me to make two lists. The first, things I can't change: Nani's health, the bills, Mummy's tiredness. The second, things I can: my study hours after dinner, reading to Nani for half an hour, telling Ms Joshi at school when it gets too much, and calling you. Since I started on the second list, I feel less like furniture and more like me.
Love,
Mehak

qa.q: What is on Mehak's list of things that can't change?
qa.a: Nani's health, the bills and Mummy's tiredness.

qa.q: What does feeling "like a piece of furniture" suggest about Mehak's state before the lists?
qa.a: Mehak felt powerless and invisible, with things happening all around and no part to play.

qa.q: Which choice helped Mehak feel less like furniture?
qa.a: Acting on the second list, study hours, reading to Nani, talking to Ms Joshi and calling Sonali, which gave back a sense of control.

qa.q: How might Sonali feel reading that their calls are on the list?
qa.a: Sonali may be touched to be part of what helps, and more understanding of the quiet calls now that the reason is clear.

grounding: A teenager in a strained household separates what cannot be changed from what can, and acting on the latter restores a sense of power.
